clinicalPearls: A rare inducible urticaria in which contact with water provokes small weals, irrespective of the water's temperature
The lesions typically resemble those of cholinergic urticaria, being small punctate weals with surrounding erythema, and characteristically appear on the neck and upper trunk
It is distinguished from aquagenic pruritus by the presence of true weals rather than itch alone, and from cold or cholinergic urticaria by independence from temperature
A water-challenge test, applying a compress at around body temperature to the upper trunk for a set time, reproduces the weals and confirms the diagnosis
Symptoms are provoked by any water contact, including bathing, swimming, rain, sweat and tears, which can make everyday life difficult
It most often begins around puberty and is usually idiopathic, with reported familial cases
Management includes non-sedating antihistamines, barrier measures before water contact and omalizumab for resistant disease
reference.pathophysiology: Aquagenic urticaria is thought to occur when water contact with the skin generates or mobilises a soluble antigen that diffuses into the epidermis and triggers mast cell degranulation with histamine release, producing weals independent of temperature. An alternative proposal is that water interacts with sebum or other skin components to form a mediator that activates mast cells. Because it is the contact with water itself rather than its temperature that provokes the reaction, even body-temperature water reliably induces lesions.
additionalDifferentials: Contact urticaria from a waterborne substance
additionalInvestigations: Water-challenge test with a body-temperature compress to the upper trunk to reproduce weals
History confirming that weals follow water contact regardless of temperature
Comparison with a cold-contact test to exclude cold urticaria
Exercise or warming provocation to exclude cholinergic urticaria where overlap exists
Skin examination to confirm true weals rather than itch alone
Assessment for coexisting inducible or spontaneous urticaria
redFlags: Any angioedema, wheeze or systemic symptoms with water contact
Extensive weals interfering substantially with bathing and daily hygiene
Diagnostic uncertainty where features overlap with cold or cholinergic urticaria
Poor response to standard therapy prompting escalation and review
reference.prognosis: Aquagenic urticaria tends to be a chronic condition, but it is usually benign and can be controlled with antihistamines, protective measures before unavoidable water contact and, in resistant cases, omalizumab; the impact on quality of life can nonetheless be considerable given the ubiquity of water.
pitfalls: Confusing it with aquagenic pruritus, which lacks weals and has different associations
Failing to control the water temperature during challenge testing, so that cold or cholinergic urticaria is not excluded
Underestimating the effect on daily life given how difficult water avoidance is
Not considering omalizumab in disabling, antihistamine-resistant disease
references: British Association of Dermatologists guidance on chronic urticaria
management: Use second-generation H1 antihistamines as first-line therapy, up-titrated as needed for symptom control
Apply barrier and protective measures such as oil-based emollients before unavoidable water contact and minimise exposure
Consider adjuncts such as anticholinergic agents or phototherapy in refractory cases
Confirm the diagnosis and monitor with water-challenge testing and assess for coexisting inducible or spontaneous urticaria
Educate the patient on triggers including bathing, swimming, rain, sweat and tears and on day-to-day self-management
